resources.string: Ambuchanania white-moss
Ambuchanania leucobryoides
Ambuchanania leucobryoides

A minute, pale Tasmanian moss that forms loose tufts on exposed quartz-rich sand. Its whitened shoots and unusual sporophyte, raised on a pseudopodium rather than a true seta, distinguish it from ordinary cushion mosses. It is a highly localized endemic of wet, acidic alpine or subalpine ground.
Endemic to Tasmania, Australia; recorded from a small number of alpine and subalpine sites.
Tiny pale moss in sparse cushions or tufts on damp, open quartz sand.
Small narrow leaves crowd the shoot tips; the whitish appearance comes from the pale foliage and exposed substrate.
Mosses do not flower. The sporophyte is elevated by a pseudopodium, not a seta.
A small capsule releases spores; reproductive structures are seasonal and may be absent.
Andreaeobryum moss
Andreaeobryum macrosporum
Andreaeobryum macrosporum

A rare northern moss growing in tight dark green tufts on persistently wet, shaded limestone or other calcareous rock. Its leaves have a strong costa and a blunt, mammillose tip. The large capsule is borne on a short seta; the species is one of the few members of the distinctive Andreaeobryaceae.
Northwestern North America, especially Alaska, Yukon and British Columbia, with scattered records farther south.
Compact moss cushions attached to damp calcareous rock, often in cool, shaded places.
Leaves are narrow and erect; a conspicuous midrib reaches a blunt, tiny nipple-like tip.
Mosses do not flower; male and female organs are borne on the leafy shoots.
A relatively large capsule on a short seta contains spores.
Black-capsuled moss
Catoscopium nigritum
Black-capsuled moss; Catoscopium nigritum

A small, dark, tuft-forming moss of calcareous flushes, wet ledges and spring margins. Its most striking field character is the nearly spherical black capsule at the end of a long red seta, giving fertile shoots a tiny club-like outline. The capsules are much more diagnostic than the minute leaves.
Arctic and northern temperate regions of Europe, Asia and North America; locally scattered farther south.
Firm dark cushions on damp base-rich soil or rock, commonly near springs.
Minute, crowded leaves form compact shoots and are less conspicuous than the sporophytes.
Mosses do not flower; the red stalk is a seta supporting the capsule.
A globose, almost black capsule is raised on a long reddish seta.
Salt-marsh pocket moss
Hennediella heimii
Salt-marsh moss; Hennediella heimii

A tiny, salt-tolerant moss of bare maritime soil, salt marsh edges and other saline ground. It often forms low reddish or olive tufts. The leaves have a distinct costa and toothed upper margins; long reddish setae carry small capsules well above the short shoots. Similar Pottiaceae require microscopic characters for confident separation.
Widespread in coastal and inland saline habitats across temperate and cool regions.
Small low tufts on exposed, saline soil that is periodically damp.
Narrow leaves have a strong midrib and small teeth near the apex.
Mosses do not flower; reddish setae emerge from the leafy tufts when fertile.
Slender capsules are carried above the shoots on long red setae.
Top-shaped bryum moss
Bryum turbinatum
Bryum turbinatum

A small moss of damp, often base-rich soil, with short leafy shoots that may be yellow-green or reddish. Fertile plants are recognized by the short, broad, pear-shaped capsule, constricted below its mouth and held on a reddish seta. Bryum species are difficult to identify without capsule and microscopic characters.
Recorded across temperate parts of Europe, Asia and North America; often local and substrate-dependent.
Short tufts or loose patches on moist soil, banks and calcareous ground.
Small lance-shaped leaves crowd the stem and taper gradually toward the tip.
Mosses do not flower; sporophytes develop from the leafy shoots.
The characteristic capsule is short, broad and pear-shaped, narrowing below its opening.
Hairpoint feather-moss
Cirriphyllum piliferum
Hairpoint feather-moss; Cirriphyllum piliferum

A pale, creeping pleurocarpous moss of woodland soil, banks and humid grassland. Its branching shoots form loose feather-like mats. Stem leaves are strongly concave and end in a long, fine hairpoint; this conspicuous tip helps separate it from similar feathermosses. Capsules are not commonly seen.
Widespread in Europe and parts of Asia; introduced or scattered in other temperate regions.
Creeping pale green mats with regularly branched, feather-like shoots.
Stem leaves are concave and taper into a long hair-like point; branches bear smaller leaves.
Mosses do not flower; reproductive organs occur at shoot tips.
Capsules are infrequent; when present they rise on a seta above the mat.
Pohlia moss
Pohlia melanodon
Pohlia melanodon

A very small moss of damp mineral soil and rock crevices. Shoots are pale green to reddish and bear narrow leaves whose costa ends below the apex. Sporophytes are occasional and have a short reddish seta with a horizontal to pendent capsule. Closely related Pohlia species can be difficult to distinguish in the field.
Scattered records in Europe and other cool temperate regions; distribution is incompletely documented.
Minute loose tufts on damp bare soil or rock, sometimes among other small mosses.
Narrow pointed leaves have a costa that usually stops short of the leaf tip.
Mosses do not flower; the reddish reproductive stalk is visible only on fertile shoots.
A small capsule may hang horizontally or downward from a short red seta.
Leafless parasitic orchid-moss
Dictyostega orobanchoides
Dictyostega orobanchoides

A small, wholly achlorophyllous mycoheterotrophic herb of humid tropical forest. It lacks green leaves and obtains carbon through fungi associated with its roots. A pale, translucent flowering stem bears a terminal cluster of tiny six-tepalled flowers; the plant can resemble a tiny broomrape, but it is a monocot in Burmanniaceae.
Tropical America, from Central America to northern South America and the Caribbean; exact range depends on taxonomic treatment.
Pale, leafless forest-floor herb emerging from moist litter, usually only when flowering.
Green leaves are absent; only small pale scales occur along the flowering stem.
Tiny pale tubular flowers have six tepals and are grouped in a terminal cyme.
A small capsule opens by three valves and releases fine seeds.
Heteranthia
Heteranthia decipiens
Heteranthia decipiens

A Brazilian herb or small subshrub in Solanaceae, with opposite leaves and delicate terminal or axillary flowering shoots. Its small bilabiate flowers have a pale lilac to whitish corolla and four didynamous stamens. The two-valved capsule and the unusual, narrow floral tube help distinguish it from superficially similar mints.
Known from southeastern Brazil, especially forested and montane areas.
Slender herb or subshrub, usually under 40 cm, growing in humid forest habitats.
Opposite simple leaves are ovate and toothed, with a visibly netted vein pattern.
Small bilabiate pale flowers have four stamens in two unequal pairs.
The dry fruit separates into two valves and contains small seeds.
Missouri foxtail cactus
Escobaria missouriensis
Missouri foxtail cactus; Missouri pincushion

A small North American cactus with a globose to flattened stem that is often partly buried. Tubercles carry clusters of fine radial spines and usually few or no central spines. Yellow to yellow-green flowers appear near the crown; small red fruits follow. A low profile and small flowers distinguish it from many larger prairie cacti.
Central North America, from the Great Plains into adjacent Canadian provinces and the southwestern United States.
Solitary or slowly clustering low cactus, often partly subterranean and only a few centimetres high.
True leaves are absent; each stem tubercle bears an areole with fine radial spines.
Small yellow to yellow-green flowers open near the stem apex.
Short red berry-like fruits mature after flowering.
Lophopyxis
Lophopyxis maingayi
Lophopyxis maingayi

A tropical woody liana and the sole species of Lophopyxidaceae. Its alternate simple leaves have conspicuous domatia—small sheltered pockets or tufts where lateral veins meet the midrib beneath the blade. Small flowers occur in axillary clusters; the distinctive dry fruit separates into winged segments. The young climbing stems should not be mistaken for a self-supporting tree.
From mainland Southeast Asia through Malesia to New Guinea and the Caroline Islands.
Woody climber in tropical lowland forest, leaning or twining through surrounding vegetation.
Alternate simple leaves bear domatia on the lower surface at the junction of midrib and lateral veins.
Small unshowy flowers are grouped in axillary inflorescences; sexes may occur on separate flowers.
A dry, segmented fruit breaks into winged units that aid dispersal.
Boorman’s paper daisy
Coronidium boormanii
Boorman’s paper daisy; Coronidium boormanii

An erect Australian perennial with woody lower stems and narrow leaves, often bearing glandular hairs. Several daisy-like heads form a terminal corymb; the papery white involucral bracts remain conspicuous around the yellow disc. Dry achenes carry a bristly pappus. The species belongs to a group of Australian paper daisies formerly placed in Helichrysum.
Endemic to southeastern Australia, in open woodland and dry forest.
Branching perennial subshrub, commonly 0.6–1.5 m tall, with erect leafy stems.
Narrow alternate leaves are mostly entire and may have small glandular hairs.
Several heads cluster at branch tips; white papery bracts surround yellow tubular florets.
Small dry achenes bear a bristly pappus for wind dispersal.
New England laurel
Cryptocarya nova-anglica
New England laurel; Cryptocarya nova-anglica

A cool-rainforest tree of the New England Tableland and nearby ranges. Its alternate, entire leaves are dark above and paler beneath; small pale flowers are borne in axillary or terminal panicles. A smooth dark drupe encloses a single seed. The species is geographically restricted and associated with high-elevation subtropical to temperate rainforest.
Northeastern New South Wales and southeastern Queensland, Australia, mainly in cool rainforest around 1,100–1,350 m.
Evergreen rainforest tree reported to reach about 20 m, often smaller at exposed sites.
Alternate leathery leaves have entire margins, a prominent midrib and a paler lower surface.
Small cream to greenish flowers grow in branched clusters; petals are absent, with six tepals.
A smooth dark drupe, ovoid to nearly spherical, contains one seed.
Pradosia decipiens
Pradosia decipiens
Pradosia decipiens

A Neotropical sapodilla-family tree with alternate, narrowly obovate to oblanceolate leaves. Its raised midrib is conspicuous on the upper surface, while small greenish flowers arise on older branches. Smooth yellowish drupes are several centimetres long. The taxonomic revision separates it from similar Pradosia by leaf venation, floral details and fruit characters.
Northern South America, in tropical forest; the documented range includes parts of the Amazonian region.
Evergreen forest tree that may reach about 20 m.
Alternate glabrous leaves are oblanceolate; the midrib is raised above and the blade narrows toward its base.
Small green flowers are borne in clusters on older woody branches.
Smooth yellowish drupes are about 3–3.5 cm long.
Pradosia kuhlmannii
Pradosia kuhlmannii
Pradosia kuhlmannii

A Brazilian rainforest tree in Sapotaceae, usually with a well-developed buttressed base. Alternate leaves are relatively small and have distinctive nearly horizontal tertiary veins. Tiny greenish flowers grow along older branches; smooth green fruits follow. These traits help distinguish it from other Pradosia with larger leaves or different venation.
Endemic to Brazil, in tropical forest regions.
Evergreen forest tree, reported to about 15 m, with a developed buttress in mature individuals.
Alternate leaves are about 4–11 cm long; tertiary veins run nearly horizontally between lateral veins.
Tiny greenish flowers occur on the branches and are easily overlooked.
Smooth green drupes develop on older branches.
Pradosia cuatrecasasii
Pradosia cuatrecasasii
Pradosia cuatrecasasii

A large Chocó-region rainforest tree with a buttressed base and unusually large leaves. The lower leaf surface is densely brown-pubescent, contrasting with the upper blade. Green flowers have a longer corolla than in several congeners; the smooth green-brown fruit is large and fleshy. This combination of broad leaves, brown underside hairs and large fruit is diagnostic.
Endemic to the humid Chocó region of western Colombia.
Large evergreen rainforest tree with substantial buttresses.
Large alternate leaves, about 20–40 cm, with dense brown hairs beneath.
Green flowers have a corolla about 7.5 mm long and occur on woody branches.
Smooth fleshy fruits reach roughly 5.5–6.5 cm and turn greenish brown.
Pradosia grisebachii
Pradosia grisebachii
Pradosia grisebachii; formerly Pradosia atroviolacea

A tropical American sapotaceous tree with alternate or loosely subverticillate, obovate to oblanceolate leaves. Paired small scales partway along the petiole are a useful diagnostic character. Small reddish flowers arise directly from older branches, followed by smooth yellowish drupes. The recent taxonomic revision places the tree-list name P. atroviolacea in synonymy with P. grisebachii.
Tropical South America, with records from northern and central regions.
Evergreen tree reported to about 15 m; mature trunks may be buttressed.
Alternate or loosely clustered leaves are 8–22 cm; paired scales occur midway along the petiole.
Small reddish flowers are borne directly on older branches (ramiflorous).
Smooth yellowish drupes follow flowering.
Jupunba obovalis
Jupunba obovalis
Jupunba obovalis; Abarema obovalis

A Caribbean legume tree with bipinnate leaves, small pale flower heads and coiled pods. The leaflet pairs are broad and obovate; mature pods become woody and twist open to expose dark seeds with vivid blue-green arils. Kew accepts Jupunba obovalis and lists Abarema obovalis as its synonym, explaining the different name in the living-tree data.
Caribbean region, including Cuba and nearby islands; recorded in seasonal woodland.
Small to medium branching tree with a spreading crown.
Alternate bipinnate leaves bear a few pairs of pinnae with broad obovate leaflets.
Small cream-white flowers cluster into rounded heads.
Curved woody pods coil as they mature; exposed seeds carry conspicuous blue arils.
Espadaea
Espadaea amoena
Espadaea amoena; Cuban espadaea

A rare Cuban woody plant of the nightshade lineage, with alternate simple leaves that are smoother above and hairy beneath. Axillary yellow-brown flowers have a short funnel-shaped corolla; the fruit is a yellow-orange berry with a pointed tip. Older Cuban floras treated Goetzeaceae separately, whereas current broad classifications place the genus within Solanaceae. Edibility reports conflict, including local warnings of toxicity: do not eat it.
Endemic to Cuba, where it occurs in dry to seasonally dry forest and scrub.
Small evergreen shrub or tree, usually only a few metres tall.
Alternate obovate leaves have a glabrous upper face and a more hairy lower face.
Axillary yellow-brown flowers have a funnel-like corolla and five-parted calyx.
A pointed yellow-orange berry follows flowering; reports of edibility conflict, so it should not be consumed.
Evans’s aglaia
Aglaia evansensis
Aglaia evansensis

A slender Fijian rainforest tree described from vegetative material. Young parts bear star-shaped hairs; leaves have three or five leaflets, with the basal pair greatly reduced and the terminal leaflet larger and blunt-tipped. The original type description did not establish flowers or fruits, so those organs are deliberately omitted from the plate and remain undocumented here rather than inferred from other Aglaia.
Endemic to northwestern Viti Levu, Fiji, in montane rainforest at roughly 900–1,180 m.
Slender evergreen shrub or tree, reported to about 8 m, in wet upland forest.
Alternate leaves have three or five leaflets; tiny basal leaflets resemble stipules and the terminal leaflet is 4–12 cm.
Species-specific flowers were not observed in the original type material; no floral details are asserted.
Species-specific fruit remains undescribed in the original account; no fruit is shown.
Apurímac tree morning-glory
Ipomoea pulcherrima
Ipomoea pulcherrima

A rare woody member of the Arborescens group, known from the Apurímac region of Peru. It is an upright shrub or small tree, not a twining vine. Broad ovate to nearly round leaves have a shallowly heart-shaped base and prominent basal veins; the young growth is softly hairy. Short inflorescences carry one, occasionally a few, long funnel-shaped flowers. The exact corolla colour is not confirmed by the sources consulted.
Endemic to Peru, known from the Apurímac Valley and seasonally dry tropical vegetation.
Upright woody shrub or small tree; unlike many morning-glories it is not a climbing vine.
Alternate broad ovate to suborbicular leaves have a shallow cordate base and prominent radiating veins.
One, rarely two or three, funnel-shaped flowers occur in short clusters; corolla colour remains uncertain.
A dry capsule follows flowering; detailed species-level fruit characters were not confirmed in the sources used.
Ambuchananiaceae
A small family of unusual mosses; Ambuchanania has a sporophyte raised on a pseudopodium rather than the usual seta.
Ambuchanania moss family
Andreaeobryaceae
A monotypic family of northern mosses adapted to cool, wet calcareous rock habitats.
Andreaeobryum moss family
Catoscopiaceae
A small moss family whose fertile shoots can carry dark capsules on reddish setae.
Catoscopium moss family
Bryaceae
A diverse moss family with small leafy shoots and usually stalked capsules; capsule form and leaf anatomy aid identification.
Bryum moss family
Brachytheciaceae
A family of creeping pleurocarpous mosses, often with regularly branched feather-like shoots.
Feather-moss family
Mielichhoferiaceae
A moss family including Pohlia; shoots are small and species identification often depends on sporophytes and microscopic characters.
Pohlia moss family
Lophopyxidaceae
A tropical family represented by a woody liana with simple leaves, domatia and segmented fruits.
Lophopyxis family
Meliaceae
A mostly tropical family of trees and shrubs, often with pinnate leaves and small flowers in axillary or terminal clusters.
Mahogany family
Sapotaceae
A mainly tropical family of trees and shrubs, often with latex, small flowers and fleshy berries or drupes.
Sapodilla family
